title: Ryan, Rigby, Przybylski 2006, The motivational pull of video games (full text, read via pdftotext)
label: research
claim: Four studies: in-game autonomy and competence predict enjoyment and preference for future play; intuitive controls matter only as gatekeeper, effect fully mediated by autonomy and competence (mostly competence); rewards used as informational feedback support autonomy, rewards used to control undermine it (cites Deci, Koestner, Ryan 1999). Study 4 (online multiplayer): relatedness also independently predicts enjoyment and future play. Correlational, self-report, short sessions.

title: Kivetz, Urminsky, Zheng 2006 goal-gradient (Columbia summary)
label: research
claim: Effort rises as proportion of distance remaining shrinks (coffee card, song-rating); engagement dips after a reward then rises toward the next; pre-stamped 'head start' card (12 stamps, 2 free) completed faster than plain 10-stamp card. Seen only via search summary, not the paper.

title: Loewenstein 1994, Psychology of Curiosity (search summaries)
label: research
claim: Curiosity arises from a perceived gap between what one knows and wants to know; later work (Golman & Loewenstein) finds information seeking higher when the gap is more important, more recently opened, and favorable news expected; a 2025 review notes not every gap elicits curiosity.

title: Deci, Koestner, Ryan 1999 meta-analysis, 128 experiments (abstract and body read via pdftotext)
label: research
claim: Expected tangible rewards undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation (engagement-contingent d=-0.40, completion-contingent -0.36, performance-contingent -0.28); unexpected tangible rewards and task-noncontingent rewards had no effect; positive (verbal) feedback enhanced free choice d=0.33 and interest d=0.31. Mostly lab tasks that were interesting to begin with.

title: Sid Meier, Just One More Turn (GDC write-up)
label: developer
claim: 'Like cliffhangers in series, tease the player enough so that he wants to see the next turn/level/corner'; 'Reward him for getting there, but focus your attention on the next thing to do'; 'A game is a series of interesting decisions' and a decision needs impact, or the belief it has. Does not give the overlapping-goals formulation.

title: Notes on Schell's interest curve
label: practitioner
claim: Schell's interest curve: an initial hook peak, then a rise with peaks and valleys to a final climax. Secondary note only; Schell's own text not seen.

title: Contextualizing Flow in Games / critiques of flow (search results)
label: opinion
claim: Flow critiqued as default paradigm for good game design (Soderman, Against Flow; Juul on failure); Csikszentmihalyi himself objected to applying flow to games; Salisbury and Tomlinson 2016 reconcile via meaning and value. No Juul text seen.

title: Thesis on Zeigarnik-type retention mechanics (search results)
label: opinion
claim: NULL: no controlled study found that interrupted or open-loop game sessions raise return rates; Zeigarnik's classic recall figures are popularly overstated; practical version is that an open loop holds attention until closed or planned. Sources were blogs and a student thesis.

title: Idle design guide and itch.io reviews (search results)
label: practitioner
claim: NULL on a minutes-based unlock cadence. Reviewers: first upgrade taking long to save for is the common early failure; a visible next-unlock condition and a fill-it-and-something-happens bar help early; pacing drags when gains are tiny relative to waiting; more players leave in the opening minutes than anywhere else.

title: Daily streak complaint threads (search results)
label: verbatim
claim: Players describe losing a long streak after a few days away as burning out; one argues rewards should be modest so people do not feel obligated. NULL: no peer-reviewed study on streak loss and churn found.

title: Loewenstein 1994, The Psychology of Curiosity (scanned PDF, OCR'd and read)
label: research
claim: Information-gap theory: curiosity arises from attention focused on a gap between what one knows and wants to know. Magnitude has absolute and relative parts; curiosity is greater toward information that more nearly closes the gap and for insight problems than incremental ones; curiosity rises with domain knowledge because a person who knows 47 of 50 frames it as the 3 missing. The 'important and recently opened' qualifier is NOT in this paper (it is later work).

title: Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng 2006, Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected (JMR), full PDF
label: research
claim: Cafe loyalty cards: interpurchase time fell 20% (0.7 days) from first to last purchase; engagement dips after the first reward. Field experiment n=108: 12-stamp card with 2 bonus stamps (same 10 purchases needed) completed in 12.7 days vs 15.6 for plain 10-stamp card (about 20% faster, p<.05). Also a song-rating site. Paper's term: illusionary goal progress.

title: Przybylski, Weinstein, Ryan & Rigby 2009 (record page; full text not available)
label: research
claim: Full abstract read; paper body behind publisher paywall (doi 10.1089/cpb.2009.0083). Abstract adds: high play time related to lower well-being only for obsessive passion; with daily-life need satisfaction controlled, the unique passion-well-being link was small.

title: Schell GDC 2009 slides (lecture copy)
label: snippet
claim: Slide for 'Chapter 14: Interest Curves' says only 'Good experiences are shaped like this' with a graph image; no text to quote. Schell's book chapter not obtained. Interest-curve shape stays secondary (notesbylex).

title: Factorio Friday Facts #300, the team's favourite parts
label: developer
claim: Kozelek: 'the mini-game of trying to fit the production lines into limited, usually uneven area'; Kovarik: progression is old improvised parts replaced by better organised high-production ones.

title: Factorio Friday Facts #309, Controversial opinions (Twinsen)
label: developer
claim: 'It's obvious that it's more fun to make your own setups'; blueprint import is 'like putting a "level up" button in an RPG' and 'could easily make a 100-hour game into an 10-hour game' (quotes re-checked 2026-11-07).

title: Software Engineering Daily 1762, Factorio with Michal Kovarik (transcript)
label: developer
claim: The core choice is 'whether investment helps you the most to move forward'; optimisation is build bigger, find the slowest component, fix it, repeat.

title: Heise interview with Satisfactory developers
label: developer
claim: 'You can make mistakes and no one will shout at you'; 'Why should we penalize players for being creative and making mistakes? Instead, we want to reward players for experimenting.'

title: Ghibellini & Meier 2025, Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects (Humanit Soc Sci Commun 12:962, open access PDF)
label: research
claim: 59 publications (38 Zeigarnik, 20 Ovsiankina, 1 both). Abstract: 'no memory advantage for unfinished tasks' but 'a general tendency to resume tasks'. Body: weighted mean recall ratio interrupted/finished 1.13 (N=7 pubs, with Zeigarnik 1927) or 1.09 (N=6, without); average effect dz=0.15 'small'; text says findings 'do not support a memory advantage for interrupted tasks when situational influences and individual differences are not accounted for'. Resumption: weighted 67.00% (N=21; 66.79% excluding Ovsiankina 1928) vs 50% chance. Mostly student lab samples, puzzle/paper tasks; none are games or apps. Authors suggest the memory effect depended on experimenter authority/task involvement, rarer today.

title: Duolingo blog: Improving the streak
label: developer
claim: One A/B test, streak separated from daily goal (one lesson extends streak) vs combined. Relative changes: Day-14 retention +3.3%, daily active learners +1%, share of daily learners on a streak +10.5% after 20 days, share of new learners on a streak +19%. Trade-off: fewer learners hit the daily goal. Post also says learners with a 7-day streak were 2.4x more likely to return next day (correlational, stated as such by the post). No n, no significance, no streak-loss or churn data. A year-later 'just over half of daily learners have 7+ day streak vs about a third' is before/after, not controlled. Company's own product, company-reported.

title: INSEAD Knowledge summary of Barasch & Silverman, On or Off Track: how (broken) streaks affect consumer decisions (J Consumer Research)
label: research
claim: Secondary summary of the paper, not the paper. Seven experiments, >4,000 participants total; one used real university fitness-programme data, the rest simulated app use (exercise logging, language learning, games). Highlighting an intact logged streak raised later engagement vs highlighting a broken one; e.g. 66.23% of intact-streak participants chose another strength exercise vs 57.86% broken. Stronger when the break was self-attributed, weaker when the streak could be repaired; almost half would watch an ad to keep/repair a streak. Authors' advice: do not highlight breaks, allow repair, broaden what counts. No effect sizes in the summary. This is a streak-break-and-engagement study the reference said did not exist; but mostly simulated, not churn.

title: Gershon: streak feedback field experiment with the one sec app (seminar abstract, via search)
label: snippet
claim: Abstract only, seen in a search summary: six-week field experiment; highlighting positive streaks kept them going, highlighting negative streaks pushed users to break them; streak feedback created new goals that competed with the original goal and raised social media use; positive streak feedback was enjoyed and improved app retention. Unpublished or seminar-stage; no n seen.

title: Salisbury & Tomlinson 2016, Reconciling Csikszentmihalyi's Broader Flow Theory: with meaning and value in digital games (ToDiGRA 2(2))
label: research
claim: The paper states that Kubey & Csikszentmihalyi (2002) 'have argued that video games are in fact likely to promote undesirable experiences' of a kind he calls 'entropy', and notes this sits uneasily with flow being applied to games. This is the authors' reading, not a quote from Csikszentmihalyi. I searched the cited Kubey & Csikszentmihalyi 2002 Scientific American article (about television) and could not confirm a passage on video games in the excerpts reached. Objection stays secondary.

title: Golman & Loewenstein 2016/2018, Information gaps: a theory of preferences regarding the presence and absence of information (Decision)
label: research
claim: Theory paper (formal model with examples; no new experiments). Defines a gap as a specific question the person is aware of. Attention to a question depends on importance, salience and surprise. Text: 'some degree of salience is a necessary, and sufficient, condition for attention, while some degree of importance is not'; one can be curious about an unimportant question ('Is that plant a fern?'). Salience raised by recent mention/priming, a knowable answer, others knowing it, contrast. Importance and salience are assumed complements (A4): more importance raises attention more for a more salient question. This is a follow-up to Loewenstein 1994, so the 'important and recently opened' claim is supported as complements, but importance is not required.

title: Koivisto & Hamari 2019, The rise of motivational information systems: a review of gamification research (IJIM 45:191-210), full PDF read
label: research
claim: Literature review, Scopus + AISeL (not other databases), 819 papers after dedup; 260 were not full papers; 273 full empirical papers analysed (105 more described future studies or systems, 84 were conceptual). Only the 66 controlled experimental quantitative studies were coded for result direction (Table 12): positive 19 (28.7%), mixed but mainly positive 31 (47.0%), null or equally positive and negative 12 (18.2%), mixed but mainly negative 2 (3.0%), negative 2 (3.0%). So 'mixed' (mixed plus null) is 45 of 66 (68%) and fully positive is under 3 in 10; the abstract's 'results in general lean towards positive findings ... the amount of mixed results is remarkable' describes this table. Education/learning (28 studies): 10 positive (35.7%), 9 mixed-positive (32.1%). Median sample size in those 66: 74.5, mean 1,165, range 1-42,724. Only 11 of the 66 test one affordance at a time (points, badges, leaderboards 4 each), so which element caused an effect is mostly unidentifiable. Of 227 quantitative-method studies only 66 were controlled experiments; most empirical gamification work has no control group. Authors' stated limits: publication bias possible (few fully negative), coding abstracted away study detail, two databases only, review coded by the first author, 'gamification is not a silver-bullet'. Counts 'mixed with positive' vs 'null' by majority of tests, not by effect size; no meta-analytic effect size is reported.

title: Przybylski, Weinstein, Ryan & Rigby 2009, Having to versus wanting to play (CyberPsychol Behav 12(5):485-492)
label: research
claim: Still abstract-level: full-text PDFs (core.ac.uk, ORCA) returned 403. Abstract and a later summary: low need satisfaction went with obsessive passion, more play, post-play tension, lower enjoyment; high need satisfaction went with harmonious passion, enjoyment and energy and did not predict hours; high play related negatively to well-being only for obsessive players. The n=1324 and sample demographics in the reference were not re-verified here.

title: Schell, Lens of the Interest Curve (gitbook transcription; fetch 401)
label: practitioner
claim: Fetch denied. Search summary of the transcription: asks whether the curve has a hook, gradually rising interest with rests between, and a grand finale; and asks the designer to compare intuition with curves playtesters draw. Gives no data. Stays a designer's lens, secondary copy, not the book itself.

title: Factorio Friday Facts #373, Space Age
label: developer
claim: Each new planet 'has its own unique theme, resource, challenges and gameplay mechanics'; goal of finishing in under 80 hours for an experienced player; 'the game was a little bit too slow and grindy, so we were speeding things up, which doesn't mean dumbing it down'; challenges 'never get too extreme'.

title: IncrementalDB review of Idle Awakening: Mage's Path
label: opinion
claim: 'I've got to praise the game's automation, which is powerful, flexible and relatively simple'; 'action lists and gathering lists let you mix and match different actions'; 'at its best as you're rolling through the first few days or weeks'; 'there's also no real sense of what to progress aside from aiming at the next unlock down the line'; 'drift into tedium as everything hits diminishing returns'; 'you can only spec into one guild at a time' (single reviewer).

title: GameBrain, Increlution player comments
label: opinion
claim: Players: 'very well paced, adds new surprising twists just as you get comfortable'; 'There aren't any interesting decisions to make; you are at best grinding out the ability to automate a task'; 'approaching each wall has some variance in what you prioritize and when'; 'no amount of optimization... will keep you from having to play the same thing'; runs of about 10-35 minutes, 'automate most of a run'. Player comments, unnamed.

title: IncrementalDB review of Increlution
label: opinion
claim: 'Automation is good, but only unlock after done it enough time'; a wrong early setup 'you need to restart all the things again'; 'a walls passing game with a skin of survival game, not for everyone'; 'a bit slow and not rewarding every prestige'. Single reviewer.

title: Upload Labs review summary (auto-generated aggregate)
label: snippet
claim: Optimizers 'troubleshoot bottlenecks'; complaints: 'need to redo layouts after unlocking new tech', 'little to do beyond waiting for numbers to increase' late, 'a number-go-up simulator'. Machine-written aggregate; weak.
